::: lead
**We are delighted to say that greta 0.6.0 is back on CRAN.**
:::

```r
install.packages("greta")
```

greta was archived from CRAN in late 2025. The short story is that greta was
doing two things CRAN does not allow: it used more than two cores by default,
and it could reach out to install TensorFlow and TensorFlow Probability onto the
machine running the checks. Both come back to the same underlying challenge,
managing greta's Python dependencies well.

So we rebuilt that part of greta from the ground up. Installation should now
*just work*, even offline, and you have far more control over which Python
backend greta uses. This post walks through what changed and what it means for
you. You can read the full list of changes in the
[release notes](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/blob/main/NEWS.md).

## The short version

- greta 0.6.0 is on CRAN again.
- The Python dependencies are now installed automatically via
  [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) on first use. For most people,
  `install_greta_deps()` is no longer a required step.
- It works offline. Once uv's cache is populated, greta can start up without an
  internet connection.
- You can choose your Python backend, persistently, with `greta_set_python()`,
  and pin your dependency versions with `greta_set_deps()`.
- MCMC now defaults to two cores and two chains, which plays nicely with CRAN
  and with laptops.
- Plenty of other bug fixes and quality-of-life improvements.

Because greta is back, its three extension packages,
[greta.gp](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta.gp),
[greta.gam](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta.gam), and
[greta.dynamics](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta.dynamics), can return to
CRAN too.

## Why greta was archived

greta sits on top of [TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/) and
[TensorFlow Probability](https://www.tensorflow.org/probability), which are
Python libraries. You can think of them a little like highly optimised linear
algebra engines: they are a big part of what makes greta fast and expressive,
and they are how greta fits MCMC efficiently. But they also mean greta has to
manage a Python installation, and getting the right combination of package
versions in place has been a genuinely hard problem.

Previously, we leaned on conda and a carefully curated table of "known good"
version combinations. The `install_greta_deps()` function did a good job of
setting all of this up, most of the time. When it worked, it was lovely. When it
did not, installation could get complicated quickly.

More recently, [reticulate](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/) gained a fast
new environment manager built on uv, which changes what a good installation
experience can look like. Rebuilding greta's installation around it is the heart
of this release.

## Installation that just works

The headline change is that greta now installs TensorFlow and TensorFlow
Probability automatically via uv the first time you use greta. You no longer
need to run `install_greta_deps()` as a separate step before you can build a
model.

Just as importantly, greta is now flexible about *which* Python environment it
uses. Instead of always forcing one managed environment, greta resolves its
backend in a sensible order: it respects a user-set `RETICULATE_PYTHON`, then a
stored greta preference, then an existing `greta-env-tf2` conda environment, and
otherwise falls back to the managed uv environment. You get convenience by
default, without giving up control.

### Offline support

This one is quietly a big deal. The managed uv backend now works **without an
internet connection**. Once reticulate's uv cache is populated, greta enables
uv's offline mode so it can start up on a plane, behind a locked-down corporate
firewall, or on an air-gapped compute node. If you want to be explicit, you can
set `UV_OFFLINE=1` to force offline resolution or `UV_OFFLINE=0` to force
online.

### Choosing your backend

Two new functions put you in the driver's seat:

- `greta_set_python()` persistently chooses which Python environment greta uses.
  You can pick the managed uv environment (`backend = "uv"`, the default), a
  conda environment (`backend = "conda"`), or a specific Python interpreter
  (`backend = "path"`). It reports the stored preference, warns you if
  `RETICULATE_PYTHON` will take precedence, and shows what greta will resolve to
  on its next load. Use `greta_reset_python()` to clear it.
- `greta_set_deps()` persistently pins which TensorFlow, TensorFlow Probability,
  and Python versions greta should use. The managed environment installs them on
  next load. Clear them with `greta_remove("deps")`.

If you point greta at a specific path, `greta_set_python("path", path = ...)`
happily accepts either a Python binary or an environment directory (a virtualenv
or conda prefix), which makes pre-installed and offline setups much easier to
wire up.

### A tidier set of helpers

Along the way we consolidated a scattering of removal and reinstall helpers.
`greta_remove()` is now the single front door for cleaning up. Via one `what`
argument it can remove the conda environment, miniconda, reticulate's uv cache,
your stored Python preference, your stored dependency versions, or all of the
above. That means `destroy_greta_deps()`, `greta_remove_all_deps()`,
`remove_greta_env()`, `remove_miniconda()`, and `remove_reticulate_uv_cache()`
are now superseded. Similarly, `reinstall_greta_env()` and
`reinstall_miniconda()` give way to `reinstall_greta_deps()`.

`greta_sitrep()` has grown to match. It now reports the resolved Python backend
and whether greta can start offline, including the `UV_OFFLINE` setting and
whether the uv cache is populated, so you can see at a glance exactly what greta
will do on its next load.

## The TensorFlow version fix

A small but crucial change: greta no longer pins TensorFlow to an exact version
in its `DESCRIPTION`. Previously we required `== 2.16.0`, which is brittle by
design; now we accept `>= 2.16.0`. Relatedly, `greta_deps_spec()` no longer
validates every combination against a fixed compatibility table. It simply
checks that the requested TensorFlow version is one greta supports (TensorFlow
2.16 and later ship Keras 3 and are not supported), and leaves the rest to uv or
conda to resolve. Less rigidity, fewer surprises.

## Friendlier defaults and smaller fixes

A few changes make everyday modelling a little nicer:

- **Sensible parallel defaults.** `n_cores` now defaults to 2 and `chains`
  defaults to 2. If you ask for more cores than you have, greta uses what is
  actually available. This also keeps greta polite on CRAN's two-core check
  machines, where we now cap TensorFlow's CPU thread pools under `R CMD check`
  and during vignette builds.
- **Clearer MCMC output.** The MCMC print method now includes warmup
  information.
- **Better display of unknown dimensions.** Reshaping a greta array with
  `dim<-` keeps the familiar `?` placeholder for unknown values instead of
  showing `NA`.
- **Tunable situation reports.** `greta_sitrep()` gains a `verbosity` argument
  with `"minimal"` (the default), `"detailed"`, and `"quiet"` levels.
- **Assorted correctness fixes.** `outer()` (and `%o%`) now works with greta
  arrays for multiplication instead of silently returning `NA`s,
  `as.unknowns()` handles plain numeric vectors, and `log()` now warns when its
  `base` argument would be ignored. Notes and messages are now emitted with
  `message()` so you can `suppressMessages()` them.

## What this means for you

If you are a returning greta user: your models are safe, the API you know is
intact, and the biggest practical change is that getting greta running should be
much less fuss than it used to be. If installation ever misbehaves,
`greta_sitrep()` will tell you what greta sees and what it will do next.

If you are new to greta: welcome! You can install it straight from CRAN, and the
Python side of things should sort itself out on first use.

```r
install.packages("greta")
library(greta)
```

## The extensions can come home too

And if you have been waiting on the extension packages,
[greta.gp](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta.gp) for Gaussian processes,
[greta.gam](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta.gam) for generalised additive
models, and [greta.dynamics](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta.dynamics) for
dynamical systems, they can now make their own way back to CRAN.
